title: OpenAI and Anthropic Tell British Lawmakers: Regulate Us
key_facts: At an evidence session of the UK parliament's cross-party Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee on Tuesday (13 Oct 2026), OpenAI and Anthropic said voluntary pledges are no longer enough and new laws should be introduced; Google DeepMind and Meta declined to back new legislation.
Liam Booth-Smith, Anthropic's head of Europe, said 'The rules should be binding' and that the company has consistently believed voluntary commitments are not enough.
Tom Duff Gordon, an OpenAI vice president, backed a statutory framework and an international convention, saying some elements should be mandatory, starting with incident reporting.
A Google DeepMind representative said the focus should be on standards; a Meta representative pointed to Britain's existing regulators, saying they were 'not writing on a blank page'.

Committee chair Liam Byrne said the aim was to show 'that you couldn't rely on voluntary self-regulation' and that he wants ministers to use Britain's coming G20 presidency to broker an international convention not dependent on the current White House.

Britain's AI Security Institute (AISI) tests frontier models before release only when companies hand them over; its director Henry de Zoete said it cannot stop a release and is 'not kite marking'; Cat Little, the top civil servant at the Cabinet Office, agreed the regime is voluntary 'at the moment'.
Anthropic's Booth-Smith said Anthropic could not give UK AISI full unrestricted access to its Mythos 5.1 model at one point, 'a question for the US government', and that AISI now has access.

The same day MI5 director Ken McCallum warned of AI's potential to change the stakes on existing or new bioweapons; four former lab researchers also gave evidence, including ex-OpenAI staffer Daniel Kokotajlo, who said companies cannot be trusted to self-regulate.
quote_evidence: Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta, both of which declined to back new legislation.
“At the moment, yes, it is,” she said.
why_it_matters_hint: Two leading AI labs publicly asked British MPs for binding rules, splitting the industry, while UK officials admitted the current regime is voluntary.
